BBC, 24 Nov 2026

Vote on Irish schools law set to fall after Stormont veto

Some £6m had been specifically earmarked for Irish-medium education

Colourful strips of paper are lying on a table. Each one has a different phrase written in Irish

A proposed law on Irish-medium education is expected to fall on Tuesday during a vote in the Northern Ireland Assembly after unionists deployed a Stormont veto.

The bill, brought forward by Sinn Féin assembly member Pat Sheehan, would require Stormont's Department of Education (DoE) to prepare a workforce plan on schools in the sector.

A vote during its final stage was postponed a fortnight ago after the Democratic Unionist Party (DUP) tabled a petition of concern with the support of other unionists.

It means the legislation will require cross-community support from a majority of both unionists and nationalists politicians in the Stormont assembly chamber in order for it to proceed.

First Minister Michelle O'Neill earlier this month accused the DUP of \"blatant disrespect\" and \"sectarianism\" over seeking to block the bill.

DUP leader Gavin Robinson had said the move was an outworking of his party's response to Sinn Féin's \"arrogance\" over the Drumcree parading dispute.

The party's Education Minister Paul Givan also said he has provided \"significant funding\" for the Irish-medium sector and the private member's bill was \"unnecessary\".

The fall-out comes after unionists criticised Sinn Féin's involvement in protests on Garvaghy Road, which blocked a contentious Orange Order parade from passing along the mainly nationalist street in Portadown, County Armagh.

O'Neill and several other senior Sinn Féin figures have been interviewed by police investigating the unnotified demonstrations, with unionists accusing the party of acting unlawfully.

Michelle O'Neill criticised the DUP's attempt to veto the legislation proposed by her Sinn Féin colleague, Pat Sheehan

Last month the DUP, which shares power with Sinn Féin in Northern Ireland's devolved government, announced it would block official engagements involving O'Neill in response to the row.

The final-stage debate for the Irish-medium Education (Workforce Plan) Bill was held earlier this month.

There were some robust exchanges in the assembly chamber, with the debate continuing for nearly three hours and ending past midnight.

A formal vote was postponed until Tuesday due to the petition of concern, which under Stormont rules triggers a 14-day \"consideration period\" before members of the legislative assembly (MLAs) can make their decision.

Earlier this month, O'Neill claimed the DUP was \"punishing children\" by seeking to veto the bill and accused the party of being \"anti-Irish in everything they do\".

Sheehan said his proposed law would require the Department of Education to \"plan properly\" to meet the needs of Irish-medium schools.

Speaking in the assembly chamber during the earlier debate, the Sinn Féin MLA accused the DUP of \"nothing but anti-Irish bigotry\".

Paul Givan said the use of the petition of concern was a \"proportionate response\"

Givan defended the DUP's use of the petition of concern, saying it was a \"proportionate response\" and his party would continue to \"hold Sinn Féin to account\".

The DUP minister said he has treated \"every single sector in education equally\" and would continue to support Irish-medium schools, describing the bill as \"unnecessary\".

\"I am already doing all of the work that is contained within this bill,\" he told the BBC's Nolan Show earlier this month.

In a further statement on Monday a DUP spokesperson said that \"schools in all sectors of our education system should be supported according to their needs\".

\"The Irish-medium sector should be part of that, but no sector should be given a priority above others,\" they added.

\"The minister has already taken significant action for Irish-medium schools and much of this bill is unnecessary given those actions.

\"We have been clear that we will use all tools available to frustrate Sinn Féin's agenda, and that includes the political virtue signalling of this bill.\"

Neon signs made for Stanley Kubrick's Eyes Wide Shut film were among the props that went under the hammer in south-west London last week.

God's Own Junk Yard also had pieces made for Tomb Raider, Bridget Jones's Diary and Elton John for sale on Thursday at its workshop on Lots Road, Fulham.

Matthew Bracey, from the family-run business, says materials used to make traditional neon are becoming harder to find as LEDs take over.

He believes neon could be worth more than gold in 10 years' time.
